30: Description: Fast and user-friendly estimation of econometric models with multiple fixed-effects. Includes ordinary least squares (OLS), instrumental variables (IV), generalized linear models (GLM), maximum likelihood estimation (ML), and the negative binomial.
31:     The core of the package is based on optimized parallel C++ code, scaling especially well for large data sets. The method to obtain the fixed-effects coefficients is based on Bergé, Butts, McDermott (2026) <doi:10.48550/arXiv.2601.21749>.
32:     Further provides tools to export and view the results of several estimations with intuitive design to change the standard-errors.

208: \item{fixef.rm}{Can be equal to "perfect_fit" (default), "singletons", "infinite_coef"
209: or "none".
210: 
211: This option controls which observations should be removed prior to the estimation.
212: If "singletons", fixed-effects associated to a single observation are removed
213: (since they perfectly explain it).
214: 
215: The value "infinite_coef" only works with GLM families with limited left hand sides (LHS)
216: and exponential link.
217: For instance the Poisson family for which the LHS cannot be lower than 0, or the logit
218: family for which the LHS lies within 0 and 1.
219: In that case the fixed-effects (FEs) with only-0 LHS would lead to infinite coefficients
220: (FE = -Inf would explain perfectly the LHS).
221: The value \code{fixef.rm="infinite_coef"} removes all observations associated to FEs with
222: infinite coefficients.
223: 
224: If "perfect_fit", it is equivalent to "singletons" and "infinite_coef" combined.
225: That means all observations that are perfectly explained by the FEs are removed.
226: 
227: If "none": no observation is removed.
228: 
229: Note that whatever the value of this options: the coefficient estimates
230: will remain the same. It only affects inference (the standard-errors).
231: 
232: The algorithm is recursive, meaning that, e.g. in the presence of several fixed-effects (FEs),
233: removing singletons in one FE can create singletons (or perfect fits) in another FE.
234: The algorithm continues until there is no singleton/perfect-fit remaining.}
235:

240: controlled by the algorithm.}

2: title: "On Standard Errors"
3: author: "Laurent Bergé, Kyle Butts"
4: date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
5: output: 
6:   html_document:
7:     theme: journal
8:     highlight: haddock
9: vignette: >
10:   %\VignetteIndexEntry{On Standard Errors}
11:   %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
12:   %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
13: ---
14: 
15: ```{r setup, include = FALSE}
16: knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE, comment = "#>")
17: Sys.setenv(lang = "en")
18: library(fixest)
19: setFixest_nthreads(1)
20: ```
21: 
22: This vignette discusses how the `fixest` package computes the standard-errors of coefficients obtained from (generalized) linear regressions (i.e. from `feols`, `feglm`/`fepois`). Please note that here we don't discuss much the *why*, but mostly the *how*.  For an introduction to the topic, see the paper by [Zeileis, Koll and Graham (2020)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sandwich/vignettes/sandwich-CL.pdf). 
23: 
24: The first part of this vignette describes the main ways standard-errors can be computed in `fixest`'s estimations. 
25: 
26: The second part discusses the nitty-gritty details about the possible choices surrounding small sample correction. 
27: 
28: The third part illustrates how to replicate standard-errors obtained from estimation methods of other software. 
29: 
30: 
31: ## Review of theory
32: 
33: The regression coefficient takes the form 
34: $$
35:   \hat{\beta} \equiv \left( X' X \right)^{-1} X' y,
36: $$
37: where $X$ is the $n \times K$ matrix of predictor variables for the sample and $y$ is the $n \times 1$ vector of the outcome variable.
38: Plugging in the working model for $y$, yields
39: 
40: $$
41:   \hat{\beta} \equiv \left( X' X \right)^{-1} X' \left( X \beta_0 + \varepsilon \right),
42: $$
43: where $\beta_0$ corresponds to the population regression coefficent and $\varepsilon$ is the $n \times 1$ vector of prediction errors. 
44: 
45: This yields:
46: $$
47:   \hat{\beta} - \beta_0 = \left( X' X \right)^{-1} X' \varepsilon.
48: $$
49: 
50: This immediately suggests the standard asymptotic distribution
51: $$
52:   \hat{\beta} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \beta_0, \left( X' X \right)^{-1} X' \Sigma X \left( X' X \right)^{-1} \right),
53: $$
54: where $\Sigma = \mathbb{E} \left[ \varepsilon \varepsilon' \right]$ is the covariance matrix of the error term. 
55: The matrix $\left( X' X \right)^{-1} X' \Sigma X \left( X' X \right)^{-1}$ is often called the "sandwich" form inspiring the name of the classic R package, [`sandwich`](https://sandwich.r-forge.r-project.org/articles/sandwich.html).
56: Continuing with the name, $\left( X' X \right)^{-1}$ show up on each side and are called the "bread". 
57: The bread is immediately estimated from the data. 
58: The "meat", $X' \Sigma X$, on the other hand is the source of all the difficulties, since we do not observe the prediction error $\varepsilon$ directly.
59: 
60: 
61: The matrix $\Sigma$ takes the form:
62: $$
63:   \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}
64:     \sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{1, 2} & \dots & \sigma{1, n} \\
65:     \sigma_{2, 1} & \sigma_{2}^2 & \dots & \sigma{2, n} \\
66:     \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
67:     \sigma_{n, 1} & \sigma_{n, 2} & \dots & \sigma_{n}^2 \\
68:   \end{bmatrix}.
69: $$
70: The elements $\sigma_{i,j}$ denote the covariance between unit $i$ and unit $j$'s error term: $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j]$. 
71: 
72: A few common cases: 
73: 
74: - "Non-correlated": If we think the error terms are non-correlated across observations, then $\sigma_{i,j} = 0$ when $i \neq j$ and $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix. 
75:   - If $\sigma_i^2 = \sigma^2$, this is called homoskedastic errors.
76:   - If $\sigma_i^2$ is allowed to vary, this is called heteroskedastic errors.
77: 
78: - "Clustering": If we think units belong to distinct clusters where errors can be correlated, i.e. $\sigma_{i,j} = 0$ when $c(i) \neq c(j)$ then $\Sigma$ is block-diagonal
79:   - If we think there are multiple clusters, then we can use "multi-way clustering" 
80: 
81: - "Autocorrelated": We might think observations "close together" have covariance, but that covariance decays with distance
82:   - "temporally autocorrelated": if distance is measured over time for a given unit (panel or time-series)
83:   - "spatially correlated": if distance is measured over space
84: 
85: There is no general answer to which setting you might be in; hence all the discussion on "how do you cluster your standard errors" or "what standard errors are you showing".
86: However, in general, we estimate standard errors by plugging in $\hat{\Sigma}$ into the sandwich form above.
87: To estimate $\hat{\Sigma}$, we use our regression residuals, $\hat{\varepsilon}$:
88: $$ 
89:   \hat{\Sigma}_{i, j} = w_{i, j} \hat{\varepsilon}_i \hat{\varepsilon}_j, 
90: $$
91: where $w_{i,j}$ is a weight term (depending on the choice of `vcov` estimator).
92: For example, if we are using "HC1" standard errors, then $w_{i,i} = 1$ and $w_{i,j} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$. 
93: For clustered standard errors, we use: $w_{i, j} = 1 / N_{c(i)}$ whenever $c(i) = c(j)$ and $w_{i,j} = 0$ otherwise.
94: 
95: Since we use $\hat{\varepsilon}_i$ instead of the true $\varepsilon_i$, it turns out that our standard error estimates will typically be too small. 
96: This problem is that the residuals tend to be "too small" because they are in-sample prediction errors (regressions overfit the sample).
97: This problem is particularly large when the sample size is too "small". 
98: Usually, we apply a "small-sample correction" to make the standard errors slightly larger.
99: These corrections are usually "ad hoc" and can vary from package to package. 
100: For this reason, we delay discussion to the end of the vignette ([hic sunt leones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here_be_dragons)).
101: 
102: 
103: #### FWL for variance-covariance matrix
104: 
105: The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem is central to the `fixest` package: we can first residualize fixed-effects from the matrix of predictors and then run a much simpler regression of $\tilde{y}$ on $\tilde{X}$ (with $\tilde{\cdot}$ representing the fixed-effect residualizing.
106: What does this due to our estimation of the fixed-effects? 
107: 
108: [Peng Ding](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167715220302480) shows that the standard Frisch-Waugh-Lovell logic applies to estimation of the variance-covariance matrix of regression coefficients (in most cases).
109: That is, we can use 
110: $$
111:   \left( \tilde{X}' \tilde{X} \right)^{-1} \tilde{X}' \hat{\Sigma} \tilde{X} \left( \tilde{X}' \tilde{X} \right)^{-1}.
112: $$
113: As long as we remember to update our degrees of freedom correction to account for the fixed-effects, our estimates will be *identical* to the "full regression".
114: Therefore, `fixest` is able to maintain its very fast estimation approach when estimating standard errors.^[This is true only if the estimator of $\hat{\Sigma}$ only depends on residuals and not the matrix $X$. This is not true of HC2/HC3 standard errors.]
115: 
116: 
117: #### Generalized linear models
118: 
119: For generalized linear models, a similar sandwich form arrives. 
120: In `fixest`, the coefficients are estimated via a ["iterative weighted least squares"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iteratively_reweighted_least_squares) procedure. 
121: Therefore, we get a similar formula as before:
122: $$
123:   \hat{V}(\hat{\beta}) = (X' W X)^{-1} (X' \Sigma X) (X' W X)^{-1},
124: $$
125: where $W$ is a diagonal $n \times n$ matrix of "working weights". 
126: Again, all the action comes into the matrix $\Sigma$.^[The $\Sigma$ is not the normal regression "residuals", but instead the *score* from the model: $(y_i - \hat{\mu}_i) \frac{\partial \eta_i}{\partial \mu_i}$. That is, it is the forecast error multiplied by the derivative of the link function.]
127: Therefore, the exact same intuition from above can be used: select the choice of vcov based on how you think error terms might be correlated to one another. 
128: 
129: 
130: 
131: ## How standard-errors are computed in `fixest`
132: 
133: There are two components defining the standard-errors in `fixest`. The main type of standard-error is given by the argument `vcov`, the small sample correction is defined by the argument `ssc`.
134: 
135: 
136: ### The argument `vcov`
137: 
138: There are three main ways to specify the VCOV using the argument `vcov`: 1) with a character string, 2) with a formula, 3) with a `vcov_*` function. 
139: When a character string, the argument `vcov` can be equal to either: `"iid"`, `"hetero"`/`"HC1"`, `"HC2"`, `"HC3"`, `"cluster"`, `"twoway"`, `"NW"`, `"DK"`, or `"conley"`. 
140: 
141: #### Classical standard errors
142: 
143: For classical standard errors, set `vcov = "iid"`.
144: This assumes that $\sigma_i^2 = \sigma^2$, i.e. the errors are non-correlated and homoskedastic. 
145: This is the default primarily for speed of estimation, but in practice it is never recommended as homoskedasticity is not likely to hold.
146: 
147: #### Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
148: 
149: There are a few options for heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, named HC1, HC2, and HC3. 
150: They all allow $\sigma_i^2$ to vary by $i$, but assumes non correlated errors across $i, j$.

28: 
29: Collinearity is the pebble that inevitably enters the shoe of any applied econometrician in the course of their work. The good news is that econometrics software take that pebble out of your shoe for you. The bad news is that sometimes this pebble is informative and tells you that something is wrong with the model you are estimating.
30: 
31: If you know what collinearity is, how software deal with it, and how it affects your coefficients, you're fine! If you're not described by the previous sentence, then two cases when you encounter collinearity.
32: Either you're lucky, and nothing happens or just a few unimportant coefficients become meaningless. Either you're unlucky and... well, your main results are wrong and your paper should be retracted.
33: 
34: Without further ado, let's try to remove chance from the econometrics process and try to understand what collinearity is and how to deal with it. 
35: 
36: 
37: # What collinearity is
38: 
39: ## This document's definitions
40: 
41: **Definitions.** We are in the context of an OLS estimation. We have one dependent variable represented by the $N$-vector $y$, and the explanatory variables represented by the $N \times K$ matrix $X$. The term *variable* can be used interchangeably with the term *column* (referring to $X$).
42: 
43: **Collinearity.** There is presence of collinearity if at least one column of the matrix $X$ is a linear combination of the other columns. 
44: Alternatively, using a more sophisticated language, there is collinearity whenever the rank of $X$ is strictly lower than $K$.
45: 
46: **Collinear set.** The collinear set is the set of all columns that are a linear combination of the other columns.
47: 
48: **Regular set.** The regular set is the set of all columns that are not a linear combination of the other columns. 
49: 
50: ## Why collinearity can be a problem
51: 
52: ### Technical reason
53: 
54: The OLS estimator is:
55: 
56: $$ \hat{\beta} = (X^\prime X)^{-1}X^\prime y $$
57: 
58: In the presence of collinearity the square matrix $X^\prime X$ is not of full rank, and hence is not invertible. This is like dividing by 0, you can't because it does not make sense. Here you cannot invert, so $\hat{\beta}$ is not defined.
59: 
60: ### Substantial reason {#subsec_FWL}
61: 
62: A good theorem to understand how OLS works is the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL) theorem.
63: 
64: Assume your set of explanatory variables is split in two: the matrix $X$ with $k_1$ columns and the matrix $Z$ with $k_2$ columns (we have $K = k_1 + k_2$). Note that you can split the variables in any way you want. The model you want to estimate is:
65: 
66: $$ y = X\beta + Z\gamma + \epsilon $$
67: 
68: Define $y^{resid}$ as the residual of $y$ on $Z$, and $X^{resid}$ as the matrix where each column is the residual of each column of $X$ on $Z$. Consider the following estimation:
69: 
70: $$ y^{resid} = X^{resid}\theta + \epsilon^{resid} $$
71: 
72: Then the theorem states that $\hat\beta = \hat\theta$ and that the residuals of the two regressions are the same. You can find an illustration below.
73: 
74: ```{r}
75: # Illustration of the FWL theorem's magic
76: 
77: # We use the `iris` data set
78: base = setNames(iris, c("y", "x", "z1", "z2", "species"))
79: 
80: library(fixest)
81: # The main estimation, we're only interested in `x`'s coefficient
82: est = feols(y ~ x + z1 + z2, base)
83: 
84: # We estimate both `y` and `x` on the other explanatory variables
85: #  and get the matrix of residuals
86: resids = feols(c(y, x) ~ z1 + z2, base) |> resid()
87: # We estimate y's residuals on x's residuals
88: est_fwl = feols.fit(resids[, 1], resids[, 2])
89: 
90: # We compare the estimates: they are identical
91: # The standards errors are also the same, modulo a constant factor
92: etable(est, est_fwl, order = "x|resid")
93: #>                                 est            est_fwl
94: #> Dependent Var.:                   y         resids[,1]
95: #> 
96: #> x                0.6508*** (0.0667)
97: #> resids[,2]                          0.6508*** (0.0660)
98: #> Constant          1.856*** (0.2508)
99: #> z1               0.7091*** (0.0567)
100: #> z2              -0.5565*** (0.1275)
101: #> _______________ ___________________ __________________
102: #> S.E. type                       IID                IID
103: #> Observations                    150                150
104: #> R2                          0.85861            0.39104
105: #> Adj. R2                     0.85571            0.39104
106: #> ---
107: #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
108: ```
109: 
110: Now let us use the theorem to understand collinearity. Take one variable from the collinear set as the focal variable. By the definition of collinearity, the residual of this variable on all other variables is a $N$-vector of 0s. Indeed, since it is a linear combination of the other variables in the collinear set, it can be perfectly explained and there is no residual. 
111: 
112: Using the FWL theorem, this means that the coefficient of this variable in the main regression is the same as the coefficient of the regression of the residual of $y$ on a constant equal to 0! This makes no sense, right. **And this is true for any variable in the collinear set!**
113: 
114: But what does that mean for *variables in the regular set?* For any such variable, the residual on all other variables contains variation, and hence the coefficient is well defined. 
115: 
116: 
117: # When is collinearity a problem?
118: 
119: Assume you have two sets of variables: focal variables for which you want to *interpret* the coefficients, and control variables for which the coefficients are not interpreted. These sets are represented by the matrices $X$ and $Z$ respectively with $k_1$ and $k_2$ columns.
120: 
121: $$ y = X\beta + Z\gamma + \epsilon $$
122: 
123: Now assume there is presence of collinearity and the model cannot be directly estimated. There are two cases. 
124: 
125: **1) The collinear set contains only control variables.** In this case collinearity is not an issue since it affects only variables that are not interpreted. The fix is easy: drop iteratively variables from the collinear set until there is no remaining collinearity (reconstruct the collinear set at each step). 
126: 
127: Note, importantly, that it is not because it affects only control variables that collinearity is fine. You should always be wary: when there is collinearity in practice when it shouldn't in theory, this is often the sign of coding mistakes (either the raw data is wrong or the processing is flawed). Allow collinearity only when it makes sense in theory (we'll cover examples later [when collinearity is fine in theory](#subsec_removal_good)).

If you are sure that the model is well specified, then check the data and fix how the variables are constructed. Now let's cover model misspecification.

131: ## The model is misspecified
132: 
133: Err... *the model is misspecified*, what does that mean? This means that you are trying to estimate stuff that don't make sense! It's like accepting the result of the following syllogism:
134: 
135: Let's add $0 = 1 - 1$ to $1 + 1$:
136: $$ 1 + 1 = 1 + 1 + (1 - 1) $$ 
137: then let's substract $2$ on both sides:
138: $$ \Leftrightarrow (1 - 1) + (1 - 1) = (1 - 1)  $$
139: and finally let's divide by the same number on both sides:
140: $$ \Leftrightarrow 1 + 1 = 1  $$
